docs.title: STATA Tutorial – Introduction to Econometrics
docs.text:
Welcome to the STATA tutorial series for the course Introduction to Econometrics. These tutorials are meant to accompany your training sessions and final exam.

Note: You don’t need to memorize these pages. The goal is a learning by doing approach — practice the commands, make mistakes, and learn by fixing them.

docs.title: 1. Getting Started with STATA
docs.text:
• What is STATA and why we use it
  • Tour of the STATA interface
  • Understanding datasets
  • Workflow: Do-files, Log files, and Data Editor
  • Basic commands and syntax
  • Your first Do-file (step-by-step explained)

docs.title: 2. Descriptive Statistics
docs.text:
• Exploring data using summary statistics
  • Understanding variable types and missing values
  • Creating and labeling new variables
  • Using summarize, tabulate, and table
  • Visualizing data with histograms, boxplots, and scatterplots
  • Cleaning data and handling inconsistent observations
  • Comparing groups (education, labor participation)
  • Log transformations and interpreting log variables
  • Creating income categories and conditional means
  • Fitting linear and LOESS curves to visualize relationships
  • Running simple and extended linear regressions with control variables

docs.title: 3. Data Exploration and Regression
docs.text:
• Load and inspect datasets
  • Create composite variables
  • Compute summary statistics by groups
  • Perform regression analysis with control variables
  • Interpret results and visualize relationships

docs.title: How to Use This Site
docs.text:
• Follow the sessions in order — each builds on the previous one.
  • Try running all the example commands yourself.
  • Remember: If you don’t open a log file at the start, your progress won’t be saved!

Happy learning!

docs.title: STATA Beginner's Tutorial: Your First Steps in Econometrics
Introduction
docs.text:
Welcome to your STATA tutorial! This guide is designed for students using STATA for the very first time in the "Introduction to Econometrics" course.

Important Note: You don't need to memorize anything in this tutorial. We follow a "Learning by doing" approach. The more training sessions you complete, the more you'll learn from understanding and fixing your mistakes.

docs.title: What is STATA?
docs.text: STATA is a powerful statistical software package that helps you understand, manage, and manipulate data.

docs.title: Why STATA?
docs.text:
• Most widely used statistical tool in the economics community worldwide
  • Always up-to-date with new econometric methods
  • Easier to learn compared to programming languages like R or Python

docs.title: STATA Interface Tour
docs.text:
Let's explore the main STATA window:

Component Purpose Menu and Toolbar Access commands via menus and shortcuts Review/History Window Shows all past commands (click to re-run) Variables Window Lists dataset variables with names and labels Properties Window Details about selected variables or dataset Results Window Displays output of commands and analyses Command Window Type commands directly for execution

docs.title: What is a Dataset?
docs.text:
A dataset is a structured collection of related data points - think of it as a super-organized spreadsheet designed for statistical analysis.

In Stata, a dataset is saved in stata format (with .dta extension), and it can only be opened in Stata.

Note: you can upload and export data in CSV, Excel and other format. To do this, you can use the menu toolbar: File→ Import and File→ Export. !

docs.title: Essential STATA Workflow
docs.text: You'll frequently use these three components:

docs.title: 1. Do File (.do file)
docs.text:
• A script file containing your STATA commands
  • Why use it? Without a do file, you lose track of your code, making debugging and navigation difficult
  • Golden Rule: Always write and run code through a do file!

docs.title: 2. Log File
docs.text:
• Records everything you do in STATA
  • Essential for troubleshooting and keeping complete session records
  • Nothing gets missed when you need to review your work
  • Records everything you do in STATA, including your commands and results. The log file is saved in plain text format.
  • Important: If you don’t open a log file at the beginning, none of your results will be saved. There’s no way to recover that output afterward.

docs.title: 3. Data Editor
docs.text:
• Built-in tool to view and edit data in tabular form
  • Useful for visual data inspection and identifying issues

docs.title: Typical Workflow:
docs.text:
1. Open STATA
  2. Start a log file (new or resume existing)
  3. Open/create your do file
  4. Write and execute code
  5. Use Data Editor and other tools as needed
  6. Save do file(s)
  7. Close log file
  8. Close STATA

docs.title: Understanding STATA Commands
docs.text:
STATA commands follow a consistent syntax pattern:

Command + Variable(s) + Options

docs.title: Examples:
docs.text:
Example 1: Basic Summary

summarize wage
  • Command: summarize (provides summary statistics)
  • Variable: wage
  • Options: None

Example 2: Scatter Plot with Title

scatter wage edu, title("Wage vs Education")
  • Command: scatter (creates scatterplot)
  • Variables: wage (y-axis), edu (x-axis)
  • Option: title(" ") (adds chart title)

Note on Variable Lists: You can often use multiple variables. For example: summarize wage edu age provides statistics for all three variables. We call wage edu age a varlist.

docs.title: Your First Do File - Complete Walkthrough
⚠️ Critical First Step: File Paths
docs.text:
The file paths in this example are specific to the instructor's computer and WILL NOT WORK on your machine!

Before running anything, you must: 1. Change the paths to match folders on your computer, OR 2. Use the cd command (recommended):

cd "C:\Users\YourName\Documents\Econometrics"

Note! Mac Users should use "slashes" instead of backslashes in the cd command

Then use shorter paths like log using "log_session_1.log"

docs.title: How to Run Code
docs.text:
• Method 1: Copy code to Command Window and press Enter
  • Method 2: Use the Do-file Editor:
  • Press Ctrl+D to run current line
  • Highlight code and press Ctrl+D to run selection
  • Click "Execute" button in toolbar

docs.title: 1. Starting the Session
docs.text:
log using "E:\009 INTRODUCTION TO ECONOMETRICS (ET4) - a.a. 2024-25\STATA session 1-20250925\Log file\log_session_1_part1.log", replace
  • Command: log using
  • Purpose: Starts recording everything in Results Window to a file
  • Option: replace overwrites existing file with same name
clear all
  • Command: clear all
  • Purpose: Clears STATA's memory - removes any loaded data and resets environment. Perfect for starting fresh.

docs.title: 2. Loading Data
docs.text:
webuse census.dta, clear
  • Command: webuse
  • Purpose: Downloads example dataset from STATA's online repository
  • Dataset: census.dta
  • Option: clear loads new dataset, dropping any current data
save "E:\009 INTRODUCTION TO ECONOMETRICS (ET4) - a.a. 2024-25\STATA session 1-20250925\Dataset\census.dta", replace
  • Command: save
  • Purpose: Saves dataset to your computer
  • Option: replace overwrites existing file

docs.title: 3. Initial Data Exploration
docs.text:
browse
  • Command: browse
  • Purpose: Opens Data Editor in view mode for visual data inspection
  • Tip: Close after checking - don't make manual changes here
describe
  • Command: describe
  • Purpose: Shows variable names, storage types, formats, and labels
  • Tip: Use describe, short for condensed output
summarize
  • Command: summarize
  • Purpose: Provides count, mean, standard deviation, min, and max for numeric variables
  • Enhanced: summarize, detail gives medians, percentiles, skewness, kurtosis

docs.title: Generating New Variables
docs.text:
generate kids_total = poplt5 + pop5_17
  • Command: generate (or gen)
  • Purpose: Creates new variable kids_total as sum of two variables
  • Important: If any value is missing (.), the result will be missing
generate has_kids = (kids_total > 0)
  • Command: generate with logical expression
  • Purpose: Creates dummy variable has_kids (1 if true, 0 if false)

docs.title: Modifying Dataset Structure
docs.text:
drop medage
  • Command: drop
  • Purpose: Permanently removes variable from dataset
  • Warning: Irreversible in current session! Save backup first if unsure.
rename (pop popurban) (population urban_population)
  • Command: rename
  • Purpose: Renames multiple variables at once
  • Tip: Use descriptive but concise names

docs.title: Advanced Variable Creation
docs.text:
gen pop_less17_more65 = poplt5 + pop5_17 + pop65p
  • Purpose: Sums three age groups
  • Alternative: Consider egen rowtotal() if you want to treat missing values as zero
gen death_r = .
replace death_r = (death/population)*1000
  • Pattern: Initialize as missing, then calculate
  • Purpose: Creates death rate per 1,000 inhabitants
  • One-line alternative: gen death_r = (death/population)*1000

docs.title: Creating Dummy Variables - Two Methods
docs.text:
* Method 1: Using replace with conditions
gen south = .
replace south = 1 if region == 3
replace south = 0 if region == 1 | region == 2 | region == 4

* Method 2: Using logical expression (Recommended)
gen south2 = (region == 3)
  • Purpose: Both create a dummy variable for southern regions
  • Preferred: Method 2 is more efficient - STATA automatically converts true to 1 and false to 0
browse region south south2
  • Purpose: Compare both methods visually to verify they produce identical results

docs.title: Variable Labels
docs.text:
label variable death_r "death rate per 1,000 inhabitants"
  • Command: label variable
  • Purpose: Adds descriptive label that appears in output tables
  • Best Practice: Always label your variables for readability

docs.title: Value Labels
docs.text:
label define region 1 "North-East" 2 "North-Centre" 3 "South" 4 "West"
label values region region
  • Command: label define + label values
  • Purpose: Maps numeric codes to meaningful text labels
  • Result: tabulate region will show text instead of numbers
label define r_south 1 "1. South" 0 "0. NE, NC, W"
label values south r_south
  • Purpose: Creates user-friendly labels for dummy variables

docs.title: Data Inspection
docs.text:
codebook region
  • Command: codebook
  • Purpose: Provides detailed variable information - counts, percentages, missing values, labels
  • Excellent for: Inspecting categorical and labeled variables

docs.title: Save Your Work
docs.text:
save "E:\009 INTRODUCTION TO ECONOMETRICS (ET4) - a.a. 2024-25\STATA session 1-20250925\Dataset\census2025.dta", replace
  • Command: save
  • Purpose: Writes current dataset to disk
  • Warning: replace overwrites without confirmation!
  • Tip: Use versioned names like census2025_v1.dta to keep backups

docs.title: End Session Properly
docs.text:
log close
  • Command: log close
  • Purpose: Closes log file and ensures all content is saved to disk
  • Important: Always close your log files!

docs.title: 💡 Pro-Tip: Comment Your Code!
docs.text:
Use comments to explain what your code does - this helps tremendously when you review your work later:

* This section creates demographic analysis variables
gen kids_total = poplt5 + pop5_17  // Total number of children
gen has_kids = (kids_total > 0)    // Dummy variable: 1 if state has any kids

* Single-line comments can use * or //
* Multi-line comments use /* ... */

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
1. Practice with the training sessions
  2. Experiment with modifying the code
  3. Make mistakes and learn from them
  4. Use the log files to track what went wrong
  5. Ask questions when you're stuck

Remember: Econometrics is learned by doing, not just by reading. Happy analyzing!

docs.title: Intro & Key Concepts
docs.text:
In this session, we will show you how to do explanatory data analysis (EDA) using descriptive statistics in STATA. The main goal here is to find insights about your data using different methods of EDA. In other words, we want to look at our data from every possible angle to understand it well before doing statistical inference. All the famous econometrics works you can find around the globe have a good and in-depth EDA sections.

Descriptive statistics help us summarize and understand our data. We use them to: - Calculate averages and typical values (mean, median) - Measure how spread out the data is (standard deviation) - Find the smallest and largest values (min, max) - Count how many cases fall into each category (frequencies)

This helps us check for errors, understand patterns, and generate hypotheses before moving to more advanced analysis.

docs.title: Learning Goals
docs.text: In this session, we will: - Learn how to explore a dataset using descriptive statistics and graphs - Understand how to clean and prepare data for analysis - Create new variables and visualize relationships - Practice interpreting numerical and graphical outputs - Run simple linear regressions with and without control variables

docs.title: 1. Getting Started
docs.text:
As always, we start from a clean slate to avoid conflicts with previous datasets.

clear all

This command removes any dataset or variable currently stored in memory.

docs.title: Opening a Log File
docs.text:
To keep a record of what you do in Stata (commands and results), always start a log file:

log using "log_stata_session2.log", replace
  • replace ensures that if a file with the same name exists, it will be overwritten
  • You can later open this .log file in any text editor or Word

docs.title: 2. Setting Your Working Directory
docs.text:
Before loading any data, Stata needs to know where your files are stored. By setting the directory at the start, you don't need to use full paths for all your do-files and folders. You simply put the directory path first, and then use this pre-set directory to navigate other files throughout your project. These steps become more important as you start working on real projects with lots of coding.

You can set the working directory in two ways:

Option 1 (Menu): Go to File → Change working directory, then select the folder where your datasets and files are stored.

Option 2 (Command):

cd "\Path"

docs.title: 3. Loading the Dataset
docs.text:
The dataset for today's exercise is Mroz.dta. It contains information on married women, including their age, education, family income, labor force participation, and wages.

If you have installed the causaldata package:

ssc install causaldata 
use causaldata mroz, clear 
save "Mroz.dta", replace

Otherwise, download it manually from Nick Huntington-Klein's GitHub or your Moodle page, save it in your working directory, and open it with:

use "Mroz.dta", clear

docs.title: 4. Getting to Know Your Data
docs.text:
Let's look at what's inside the dataset.

describe

This command lists all variables, their storage type, labels, and number of observations.

You should recognize variables such as: - lfp: labor force participation (1 if working, 0 otherwise) - age: woman's age - wc: college education dummy (1 if college graduate) - lwg: log of wage - inc: family income - k5, k618: number of children under 5 and aged 6–18

Now let's get more detailed information:

codebook

Some variables in Stata have string values, but when you used “describe” command, the storage type of the variable might appear as a byte

This happens because the variable is numeric, but has value labels.

In order to know the numeric value, you need to check the codebook of that variable.

For example, here from session 2 we have the variable wc with label “Wife’s college attendence” , the values shown in the data editor were “Wife did not attend college” and “Wife attended college”

However, when you check the codebook, you will see the numeric values. Here for wc we

wc = 0 → “Wife did not attend college”

wc = 1 → “Wife attended college”

You need to know this numeric values if you want to clean or transform the data, or when using logical conditions

💡 Always check variable labels carefully. this helps avoid confusion later.

docs.title: 5. Understanding Variable Types
docs.text:
In econometrics, we work with different types of variables:

  • Continuous variables (like age, inc, lwg): Can take on many numeric values
  • Categorical/Binary variables (like lfp, wc): Take on limited values, usually categories or yes/no

We use different commands for different variable types, as you'll see in the next sections.

docs.title: 6. Checking for Missing Values
docs.text:
Real data often has missing values, which Stata marks with a dot (.). Let's check if our dataset has any missing values: 

misstable summarize

Alternatively, you can use: 

summarize, detail

Look for variables with very low counts; this might indicate missing data. When we use keep if or drop if commands later, Stata will automatically exclude observations with missing values in those variables.

docs.title: 7. Creating a Working Copy
docs.text:
Before we start cleaning and modifying the data, let's preserve the original dataset by creating a working copy:

save "Mroz_working.dta", replace

Now all our changes will be saved to this working file, keeping the original data safe.

docs.title: 8. Summary Statistics
docs.text:
Let's explore our variables using summary statistics.

For continuous variables (like age, income):

summarize age

This gives you: - Mean: the average age - Std. Dev.: how spread out ages are - Min/Max: the youngest and oldest women in the sample

For more detailed information:

summarize age, detail

This adds the median (middle value), percentiles, and information about the distribution. The median is often better than the mean when data has extreme values.

For categorical variables (like labor force participation):

tabulate lfp

This displays the number and percentage of women who work (lfp = 1) and those who don't (lfp = 0).

💡 The tabulate command is essential for exploring categorical variables (binary or discrete).

docs.title: 9. Creating New Variables
docs.text:
The dataset has two variables for children: - k5: children under age 5 - k618: children aged 6 to 18

Let's combine them into one total count:

gen n_children = k5 + k618

Now let's look at the distribution:

tabulate n_children

This shows us how many families have 0, 1, 2, etc. children, which is more informative than just the average.

docs.title: 10. Labeling Variables
docs.text:
To make your dataset readable and presentable:

label var n_children "Total number of children"

Good labeling helps you and others understand what each variable represents.

⚠️ Reminder: In Stata, there are two kinds of labels:

Variable labels — describe what the variable means Example: age → “Respondent’s age”

Value labels — describe what each numeric value represents within a variable Example: 1 = Yes, 0 = No

For more details on STATA variable types, see the Annex: STATA Variable Types at the end of this document.

docs.title: 11. Basic Visualizations
docs.text:
Graphs help us see patterns that numbers alone might miss.

For distributions of continuous variables:

histogram wage, frequency

This shows the shape of the wage distribution , is it normal? Skewed?

For comparing groups (categorical vs continuous):

graph box wage, over(wc)

This boxplot shows how wages compare between college graduates (wc = 1) and non-graduates (wc = 0). It displays the median, spread, and any unusual values.

For relationships between two continuous variables:

scatter inc wage

This creates a scatterplot, where each point is one woman. Look for the overall pattern: "do higher-income families correspond to higher wages?"

docs.title: 12. Data Cleaning
docs.text:
Now let's focus our analysis on working women:

keep if lfp == 1

After this command, your dataset will only contain women who are working (lfp = 1).

Check your data for unrealistic values:

summarize

If you notice negative family income, that's not reasonable, so we remove those observations:

drop if inc < 0

⚠️ Always double-check before dropping data! You can inspect outliers with:

list inc if inc < 0

docs.title: 13. Wages and Education
docs.text:
Let's explore how education relates to earnings. The variable wc indicates whether a woman has a college education (1 = yes, 0 = no). The variable lwg represents the log of the wage.

Let's compare average log-wages across education levels:

summarize lwg if wc == 0
summarize lwg if wc == 1

Or use one command to summarize both groups together:

table wc, stat(freq) stat(mean lwg)

💡 Remember: "log-wage" is in logarithmic scale. The difference in log-wages can be interpreted as a percentage difference in average wages.

docs.title: 14. From Log-Wage to Actual Wage
docs.text:
We can convert log-wages back into real wages using the exponential function:

gen wage = exp(lwg)

Now repeat the comparison:

summarize wage if wc == 0
summarize wage if wc == 1
table wc, stat(freq) stat(mean wage)

This gives the average wage in actual monetary units, making the results easier to interpret.

docs.title: 15. Log Transformations
docs.text:
Sometimes variables like income and wages are very skewed. To make relationships more linear and interpretable, we log-transform income:

gen linc = log(inc)

Then plot the relationship again:

scatter linc lwg

You should now see a clearer linear relationship.

docs.title: 16. Exporting Graphs
docs.text:
To save a graph that's currently open:

graph export "ex1_graph1.png", replace

This saves it in your working directory as a .png image.

docs.title: 17. Conditional Means: Binning by Income
docs.text:
Let's group income into 10 categories and compute average wage within each group:

egen inc_cat = cut(inc), group(10) label
table inc_cat, stat(mean wage)

You now have a simple nonparametric summary , the mean wage for each income decile.

docs.title: 18. Smoothed Relationships (LOESS)
docs.text:
To visualize a smooth curve that shows the average trend:

lowess linc lwg

This nonparametric regression (LOESS) fits a smooth line through the scatterplot.

docs.title: 19. Combine Graphs
docs.text:
We can combine: - A scatterplot (raw data), - A linear regression fit, and - A LOESS smooth curve:

twoway lfit linc lwg || lowess linc lwg || scatter linc lwg
graph export "ex1_graph2.png", replace

This gives a full picture: - Blue line: linear fit - Red line: LOESS smooth - Dots: observed data points

docs.title: 20. Labeling Categories
docs.text:
To make your income categories readable:

label var inc_cat "Income category"
label define inc_cat_lb 0 "less 9k" 1 "between 9k and 10.95k" 2 "between 10.95k and 13.3k" 3 "between 13.3k and 14.9k" 4 "between 14.9k and 17.09k" 5 "between 17.09k and 18.56k" 6 "between 18.56k and 21.16k" 7 "between 21.16k and 25.2k" 8 "between 25.2k and 31.8k" 9 "more 31.8k", replace
label values inc_cat inc_cat_lb

docs.title: 21. Simple Linear Regression
docs.text:
Now let's model the relationship between log-wage and log-income:

reg lwg linc

The output tells you: - The estimated coefficient on linc: interpreted as elasticity (a 1% increase in income → β% increase in wage) - R-squared: how much variation in wages is explained by income alone - _cons: the constant term (predicted wage when income is zero)

💡 Important: An elasticity tells us the percentage change in one variable (wage) given a 1% change in another variable (income).

docs.title: 22. Adding Control Variables
docs.text:
To make your regression more realistic, add controls for: - Age and its squared term (to capture nonlinear effects) - Education (wc) - Number of children (n_children)

reg lwg linc c.age##c.age wc n_children

Interpretation: - The sign and size of linc show the partial relationship between income and wage, holding other factors constant - The age and age² terms capture how wages vary across the life cycle - wc shows how college education affects wages

⚠️ Correlation is not Causation! This regression shows a relationship between income and wage, but it does not prove that higher income causes higher wages. There could be omitted variables (like ability, experience, or industry) that influence both. We add control variables to try and account for this, but we must always be cautious in our interpretation.

docs.title: 23. Saving Your Work
docs.text:
Once finished, save your dataset with all new variables and cleaned data:

save "Mroz_session2.dta", replace
log close

Congratulations! You've completed a comprehensive exploratory data analysis and are ready for more advanced econometric techniques.

Annex: STATA Variable Types

This annex provides a quick reference for STATA variable types. It summarizes the storage types, capacities, and examples of variables you may encounter in datasets. Use this table when creating, importing, or inspecting variables to ensure correct data handling.

Type Storage Size Meaning / Capacity Example Variable Example Value Numeric byte 1 byte Whole numbers from -127 to 100 age_group 5 int 2 bytes Whole numbers from -32,767 to 32,740 year 1999 long 4 bytes Whole numbers up to ±2 billion population 1,250,000 float 4 bytes Decimal numbers (≈7 digits precision) income 15,342.56 double 8 bytes Decimal numbers (≈16 digits precision) gdp 52,345.6789012 String str1 1 byte Text up to 1 character gender "M" str2 2 bytes Text up to 2 characters code "AB" str3 3 bytes Text up to 3 characters abbr "USA" str# # bytes Text up to # characters (e.g., str10 = 10 chars) name "Michael" str2045 2045 bytes Text up to 2045 characters comment "This is a very long text..." strL Variable Text up to ~2 billion characters notes "Detailed report on the observation..."

💡 Note: Selecting the correct variable type ensures efficient memory usage and prevents rounding or truncation errors in STATA.

docs.title: STATA Tutorial – Session 3: Data Exploration and Regression Practice
docs.text: 📌 Note:  All the full STATA codes used in this tutorial, together with training exercises and questions, are available for download on your Moodle page. Be sure to retrieve them so you can follow along and practice.

docs.title: Introduction & Motivation
docs.text:
In this session, we continue building your skills in exploratory data analysis (EDA) and regression modeling. This exercises push you beyond simple summary statistics: you will create new variables, explore relationships with tabulations and regressions, test for nonlinear patterns, and interpret results in context. The goal is that by the end, you feel comfortable exploring real datasets, diagnosing patterns, and modeling relationships with control variables and interactions.

We’ll work with two datasets in two parts:

  • Part 1: hsbdemo.dta — data on high school students (grades, school types, programs, socioeconomic status)
  • Part 2: restaurant_inspections.dta — data on restaurant health inspection scores and number of locations

As usual, we will walk step by step, explaining why we run each command, what the output means, and what to watch out for.

docs.title: 1. Load the Dataset and Inspect Variables
docs.text:
use "hsbdemo.dta", clear describe codebook female ses schtyp prog
  • use ... , clear loads the dataset and clears any existing memory.
  • describe gives you variable names, types, labels, and counts.
  • codebook (for selected variables) shows you unique values, missing counts, and distributions.

At this point, you should check: - What coding scheme is used (e.g. is female = 0/1? What values does schtyp take?). be careful and check if the variable have numeric values only or numeric and labels). - Which values of prog (program) exist — e.g. academic, general, vocational and the numeric value of each one.

docs.title: 2. Create an Overall “Score” Variable
docs.text:
We want a new variable score that is the average of five subject grades: read, write, math, science, socst. 

gen score = (read + write + math + science + socst) / 5 
label variable score "mean score"
  • gen score = … creates the new variable.
  • We divide by 5 because there are five subjects.
  • label variable gives a human-readable label for output display.

Another, more robust way to write it by using rowmean:

gen score = rowmean(read + write + math + science + socst)
label variable score "mean score"

Why do this? Because having a single composite score simplifies analysis (fewer regressions) and gives you a summary measure of each student’s performance.

docs.title: 3. Compute Averages by Gender (and Overall)
docs.text:
We’d like to know how male vs. female students perform, and also the overall average.

*Overall summary
summarize score

*Summary by gender
bysort female: summarize score

*another way to get the summary by gender
summarize score if female == 0
summarize score if female == 1
  • bysort female: summarize score runs the summary (mean, sd, min, max) separately for female = 0 and female = 1.
  • The summarize … if … lines isolate each group explicitly.
  • A final summarize gives you the overall average.

From the output, note the mean score for males, for females, and overall. Are there noticeable differences?

⚠️ Make sure to check the number of observations in each group — differences might be due to sample sizes or missing data.

docs.title: 4. Tabulate Program by School Type
docs.text:
We want two types of information:

  1. Within private schools, what percentage of students attend an academic program?
  2. Among students in academic programs, what share come from private schools?
tab schtyp prog, row 
tab schtyp prog, col
  • tab … , row gives row percentages (i.e. within each schtyp, the distribution of prog).
  • tab … , col gives column percentages (i.e. among each prog category, the distribution of schtyp).

Interpret carefully:

  • From the row table, read across a school type to see what proportion of its students are in each program.
  • From the col table, read down a program to see how many come from each school type.

docs.title: 5. Percentage of Students Enrolled in English (within Public Schools)
docs.text:
The question is: within public schools, what fraction of students are enrolled in an English/honors program?

tab schtyp honors, row

Here, reading the row for schtyp = public gives you the proportion enrolled in honors within public schools.

docs.title: 6. Regression: Program Type → Mean Score
docs.text:
We now ask: does the type of educational program a student attends predict their average score?

reg score i.prog
  • i.prog tells STATA to treat prog as a categorical (factor) variable, creating dummy variables for each program (omitting one as baseline again check the codebook to see which category is listed as the first).
  • The regression output gives coefficients for each non-baseline program: how much higher (or lower) their average score is, relative to the baseline, holding nothing else constant.

Check: - Which program is the omitted (baseline) category? - Are coefficient estimates statistically significant? - What does the constant _cons represent (the expected score in the omitted program)?

Now let's interpret the results together:

- We have the baseline here is the general category, both of academic and vocation are relative to general - Students who are in academic program score on average ~5.10 points higher, while for students who are in vocational program average score ~4.50 points lower. Both of the coefficients are statistically significant at the 1% level (p<0.01). - Intercept: The mean score for students who are enrolled in general program is 50.83 - R-squared: 24.6% of variation in mean scores explained by the program type alone.

docs.title: 7. Regression with Controls: SES & School Type
docs.text:
We expand the model, adding socioeconomic status (ses) and school type (schtyp) to control for background differences:

reg score i.prog i.ses i.schtyp

With control variables, you can see: - Whether the gaps across prog categories shrink or persist after controlling for SES and school type. - The estimated effect of SES categories and being in a private vs public school on the mean score (relative to omitted reference groups).

Interpretation steps:

  1. Look at each i.prog coefficient: is it still large after controls?
  2. Look at i.ses and i.schtyp: which levels are significant, and in which direction?
  3. Does the model’s R² increase substantially (i.e. do controls explain more of the variation)?

let's interpret it together: We adding the socioeconomic and school type variables to the above model:

  • The coefficient for the academic slightly deceases to ~4.08 but still positive and statistically significant, same for vocational, the coefficient remains negative ~-4.81 and statistically significant. This conclude that students who are enrolled in academic programs outperform those in general programs and students in general programs outperform those who are in vocational program

  • Students from middle and high SES outperform students coming from low SES by 3.4 and 5.7 score, respectively. This highlight the strong positive influence of socioeconomic status on academic performance.

  • The type of school doesn’t effect the score as the coefficient of private school is small and not significant (p = .734)

  • Looking at the R-squared, the model explained ~31% of the score variation, which represents a moderate improvement in the explanatory compared to the simpler model.

docs.title: 8. Predicted Mean Scores for Specific Profiles
docs.text:
We want to compute predicted average scores for students in different programs, conditional on being in a private school and having high SES.

margins prog, at(schtyp = 2 ses = 3)
  • at(...) fixes schtyp and ses at specific values.
  • This gives you predicted means of score by prog, holding school type and SES constant.

Interpretation:

  • Suppose schtyp=2 corresponds to private school, and ses=3 to high SES. Then you’re comparing predicted scores across programs within those conditions.
  • You can compare which program yields the highest expected score for that profile.

docs.title: 1. Load Restaurant Data
docs.text:
use "restaurant_inspections.dta", clear

Make sure your working directory is correct so STATA finds the file.

docs.title: 2. Reproduce Table 13.2 Regressions
docs.text:
We run two regressions on health inspection scores (inspection_score) and number of locations (numberoflocations):

reg inspection_score numberoflocations 
estimates store m1  

reg inspection_score numberoflocations year 
estimates store m2
  • The first regression is the bivariate relationship.
  • The second adds a control for year to see whether time effects change the estimate.

docs.title: 3. Export Regression Table
docs.text:
esttab m1 m2 using "regression_table.doc", se r2 ar2 replace
  • esttab (from estout package) neatly formats regression results into a Word .doc file.
  • You include standard errors (se), R² (r2), and adjusted R² (ar2).

If not installed yet, run:

ssc install estout
  • You can always ask a LLM model (for example, chatgpt) to help you create the table showing the results of the two regression.

    Example Prompt: Act as a Stata specialist. I have already run these two models: reg inspection_score numberoflocations reg inspection_score numberoflocations year Please provide the Stata command to combine the results from both of the above regressions into one table (side by side) showing coefficients, robust standard errors, R-squared, N, and significance stars. Then, I want to save that table in my current working directory as RTF (for Word).

docs.title: 4. Check for Nonlinearity in Number of Locations
docs.text:
We suspect the relationship may not be purely linear. Let's allow for a quadratic term:

gen numloc2 = numberoflocations^2 
reg inspection_score numberoflocations numloc2

Alternatively, more elegantly:

reg inspection_score c.numberoflocations##c.numberoflocations
  • c.var##c.var creates both the linear and squared term automatically.
  • Check whether the coefficient on the squared term is significant, and examine the sign (positive or negative curvature).

  • If the squared term is significant and negative, the relationship may be concave (diminishing returns).

  • Read lecture #5 and chapter 13.2 for more context.

docs.title: 5. Marginal Effects of Locations
docs.text:
We want to know how marginal changes in number of locations affect inspection scores:

margins, dydx(numberoflocations) 
margins, dydx(numberoflocations) at(numberoflocations = 100)
margins, dydx(numberoflocations) at(numberoflocations = 750)
  • The first margins gives an average marginal effect.
  • The others compute marginal effects at specific values (e.g. for small or large chains).
  • You can plot these with marginsplot to visualize how the effect evolves.

docs.title: 6. Interaction with Weekend Inspections
docs.text:
We might think that inspections done on weekends behave differently. To test this:

reg inspection_score c.numberoflocations##i.weekend year, robust 
margins, dydx(numberoflocations) at(weekend = 1) 
margins, dydx(numberoflocations) at(weekend = 0)
  • c.var##i.var lets you interact a continuous variable with a categorical one (here, weekend).
  • robust gives robust standard errors (helpful with heteroskedasticity).
  • margins, dydx(...) at(...) gives how the slope (effect of number of locations) differs on weekends vs non-weekends.

Interpretation:

  • Does the number-of-locations slope differ on weekends?
  • Which group has steeper slope — weekend or non-weekend?
  • Are differences statistically meaningful?

If you look at your regression table you can find:

  • On weekends

    • Each additional restaurant location is associated with a negative effect on the inspection score by -0.029 points. And the effect is statistically significant (p = 0.008). The confidence interval (–0.05 to –0.0075) means we’re 95% confident the true effect lies within that range is always negative.

  • On weekdays

    • Each additional location decreases inspection scores by about 0.019 points, this effect is highly significant (p < 0.001) and very precisely estimated (small standard error).

  • Comparison (weekend vs. weekday)

    • The effect of having more locations is slightly more negative on weekends (–0.029 vs –0.019), but not dramatically so. Since the interaction term in the regression numberoflocations#weekend wasn’t statistically significant (p = 0.369), we can conclude that this small difference is not statistically meaningful.

    • This means: The negative relationship between the number of locations and inspection score is essentially the same on weekends and weekdays.

docs.title: Conceptual Takeaways & Guidance
docs.text:
• Descriptive statistics and tabulations (summaries, tab) help you see patterns, spot anomalies, and form hypotheses.
  • Regression formalizes a relationship by estimating a “line of best fit” while controlling for other factors.
  • Nonlinear models (quadratic, interactions) allow more flexibility: you are not locked into straight-line assumptions.
  • Marginal effects and margins are your friend — they translate coefficient estimates into more interpretable quantities (how much a small change in X affects Y).
  • Always inspect, think, question — e.g. look at sample sizes, variable coding, potential outliers, and whether causality can be claimed.

docs.title: STATA Tutorial – Session 4: Panel Methods & Fixed Effects (Balanced Panel 1997–2000)
docs.text: 📌 Note:  All the full STATA codes used in this tutorial, together with training exercises and questions, are available for download on your Moodle page. Be sure to retrieve them so you can follow along and practice.

docs.title: Motivation & Learning Goals (Short)
docs.text:
In this session, we work through an applied panel example: what determines airfares on routes over time. You will:

  • compute the within (demeaned) transformation by hand (manual FE method);
  • estimate Fixed Effects both manually and with xtreg, fe;
  • add year dummies (two-way fixed effects);
  • interpret coefficients (especially the market share and passengers effects);
  • learn why time-invariant regressors (distance) vanish under route FE;
  • and compare within R^2 from different specifications.

docs.title: Data & Model (Reminder)
docs.text:
A panel dataset (or longitudinal dataset) contains observations on multiple entities (e.g., airline routes) across several time periods. This structure allows us to study changes within each entity over time and control for unobserved, time-invariant characteristics. In our case, each route is observed annually from 1997 to 2000, and we model how fares depend on route-specific factors and yearly trends.

You analyze a balanced panel for routes i over years t = 1997–2000. The dependent variable is log of average one-way fare:

Key points:

  • bmktshr: market share of the biggest carrier on route i in year t (time varying).
  • dist: distance (miles) between origin and destination (time invariant).
  • passengers: average passengers on route i in year t (time varying).
  • y98, y99, y00: year dummies.
  • alpha_i: unobserved route fixed effect.
  • u_it: idiosyncratic error.

docs.title: 0 — Start Clean, Set Working Directory, and Open a Log
docs.text:
clear all
cd "E:\009 INTRODUCTION TO ECONOMETRICS (ET4) - a.a. 2025-26\STATA session 4-20251016"
log using "log_session_airfare_4.log", replace
  • clear all avoids any leftover objects.
  • log using ... replace keeps a timestamped record of commands and output.

docs.title: 1 — Load the Dataset and (Optionally) Rename Variables
docs.text:
use "AIRFARE.dta", clear

* optional friendly renames (helps later)
rename id route_id
rename fare avg_fare
rename dist distance_miles
rename passen passengers_day
rename bmktshr bigcarrier_share
rename concen market_conc

After loading, always inspect structure:

describe
summarize
codebook route_id avg_fare distance_miles passengers_day bigcarrier_share

Check now: Are there missing values? Is the panel balanced? Is route_id unique per route? Count observations per route:

bysort route_id: gen n_obs = _N
tabulate n_obs

A balanced panel should show the same n_obs for all routes (expected = 4 years).

docs.title: 2 — Create Clear Logged Variables
docs.text:
Use descriptive names. Log transforms are commonly used for skewed variables and to interpret coefficients as elasticities.

gen log_fare = ln(avg_fare)
gen log_distance = ln(distance_miles)
gen log_distance2 = log_distance^2
gen log_passengers = ln(passengers_day)

Check basic summaries (means, sds, min/max) and look for zeros or negatives before logging:

summarize avg_fare distance_miles passengers_day
count if avg_fare <= 0 | distance_miles <= 0 | passengers_day <= 0

⚠️ If any of these counts > 0, investigate: logs are undefined for non-positive values. Fix or drop problematic observations with care.

docs.title: 3 — Fixed Effects (Manual / “Book” Method)
docs.text: The manual within transformation is a great exercise to understand FE intuition: remove each route’s mean to eliminate alpha_i.

docs.title: 3.a Compute route means (time averages) for the outcome and time-varying regressors
docs.text:
by route_id: egen fare_mean = mean(log_fare)
by route_id: egen share_mean = mean(bigcarrier_share)
by route_id: egen pass_mean = mean(log_passengers)

(We do not compute a mean for log_distance because it is time-invariant; its within value would be zero.)

docs.title: 3.b Create demeaned (within) variables
docs.text:
Demean each time-varying variable by subtracting the route mean:

gen fare_within = log_fare - fare_mean
gen share_within = bigcarrier_share - share_mean
gen pass_within = log_passengers - pass_mean

Check that the within variables sum to (approximately) zero by route:

by route_id: egen check_sum = sum(fare_within)
summarize check_sum

(You should see near-zero sums — numerical precision may produce tiny nonzero values.)

docs.title: 3.c Estimate OLS on the within-transformed data
docs.text:
Now run the OLS regression using only within variables (this is the manual FE / "book" estimator):

reg fare_within share_within pass_within

Interpretation tasks:

  • beta 1 (coefficient on share_within): measures whether increases in the big carrier’s market share (relative to that route’s average share across years) are associated with increases/decreases in log fare (relative to the route’s time mean). A positive beta 1 means that when the big carrier gains share on a route (relative to that route’s mean), fares rise.
  • beta 2 (coefficient on pass_within): measures whether increases in log passengers (relative to that route’s mean) affect fares. Positive beta 2 means that more passengers → higher fares (within that route over time); negative would indicate the opposite.

Which variation is used?

This regression uses within-route (time variation) only. Cross-route (between) variation is removed by demeaning.

docs.title: 4 — Manual within + Year Dummies
docs.text:
Year dummies capture common shocks across all routes in a year (e.g., oil price shocks, regulation changes).

reg fare_within share_within pass_within i.year

Questions to answer from output:

  1. What do the coefficients on i.year represent? They show average deviations in log fares for each year (relative to the omitted year — usually 1997), after removing route means and conditional on the within variation in share and passengers. In other words, they capture common time effects (year shocks) across routes.
  2. Why add time dummies? To control for factors that change over time and affect all routes (or many routes) simultaneously. Omitting them can bias coefficients if those time shocks correlate with regressors (e.g., market share systematically changes with industry-wide shocks).
  3. Compare bmktshr (share) coefficient before/after year dummies: Did it change? If yes, that suggests part of the raw within relationship was due to common time shocks correlated with share. If not, the share effect is robust to controlling for year effects.

docs.title: 5 — Fixed Effects Using Stata’s xtreg, fe (the Built-in Within Estimator)
docs.text: This should give identical estimates (up to numerical precision) to your manual within OLS.

docs.title: 5.a Declare the panel
docs.text:
xtset route_id year

Check for panel settings and whether any gaps exist.

docs.title: 5.b Estimate FE with xtreg
docs.text:
xtreg log_fare bigcarrier_share log_passengers, fe

Compare to manual method:

The xtreg, fe coefficients on bigcarrier_share and log_passengers should match the coefficients from the manual within regression (assuming the same variables and no year dummies). If they match, your manual demeaning was done correctly.

docs.title: Why add log_distance now?
docs.text:
xtreg log_fare bigcarrier_share log_distance log_distance2 log_passengers, fe

What happens to log_distance and log_distance2?

Because log_distance (and its square) are time invariant for each route, they are perfectly collinear with the route fixed effect alpha i. The within (demeaning) transformation subtracts the route time mean, leaving zero variation for time-invariant regressors — thus xtreg, fe drops them from the estimation (STATA will report they are omitted).

This is why a fixed-effects (within) estimator cannot estimate coefficients on variables that do not vary over time within units.

docs.title: 6 — Fixed Effects + Year Dummies (Two-way FE)
docs.text:
Include both route FE and year FE — a common specification to control for both route fixed heterogeneity and common time shocks.

xtreg log_fare bigcarrier_share log_passengers i.year, fe

docs.title: 6.a Compare R^2 (within) across models
docs.text:
xtreg reports several R^2 measures; the relevant one here is within R^2 (how well the model explains variation within routes).

Compare:

  • One-way FE (route only): xtreg ... , fe without i.year → within R^2 = R^2_{oneway}.
  • Two-way FE (route + year): xtreg ... i.year, fe → within R2 = R2_{twoway}.

Interpretation of change in within R^2:

If adding year dummies increases within R^2, common time effects explain additional within-unit variation (e.g., year shocks that differ from route means).

docs.title: 6.b Add distance and distance squared to the model, then explain
docs.text:
xtreg log_fare bigcarrier_share log_passengers log_distance log_distance2 i.year, fe

Here again log_distance and log_distance2 are time invariant and will be dropped by xtreg, fe.

Why? Because the within transformation eliminates time-invariant components — there is no within variation left to estimate their effect.

docs.title: 7 — Answers / Guidance to the Numbered Questions (Compact but Explicit)
docs.text: Task Guidance Load the dataset Done in §1. Create logs Done in §2 (log_fare, log_distance, log_distance2, log_passengers). Manual FE (book method) You computed route means and demeaned time-varying variables in §3.a–§3.b. OLS on demeaned variables in §3.c. Interpretation of beta_1 (share) If beta_1 > 0, within a route, when the big carrier’s share is higher than its route average, fares tend to be higher. Interpretation of beta_2 (passengers) As log_passengers changes, beta_2 is an elasticity: e.g., beta_2 = 0.1 means a 1% increase in passengers (within that route over time) is associated with a 0.1% increase in fare. Type of variation Within-route (time variation) only. Manual FE + year dummies Year coefficients represent average (common) deviations in log fares in those years (after removing route means). Year dummies are important to control for industry-wide shocks correlated with regressors. xtset & xtreg, fe xtset route_id year declares the panel. xtreg ... , fe implements the within estimator — results should match the manual method. Why does log_distance disappear? Because it is time-invariant: the within transform subtracts the route mean and leaves zero for that regressor. xtreg + year dummies Estimate with i.year. Compare within R^2 of one-way (route only) vs two-way (route + year) — interpret as explained earlier (§6.a).

docs.title: Useful Additional Commands & Checks (Practical Checklist)
docs.text:
Compare manual vs xtreg coefficients numerically:

* manual (run earlier)
reg fare_within share_within pass_within
estimates store manual_fe

* xtreg
xtreg log_fare bigcarrier_share log_passengers, fe
estimates store xt_fe

* compare
esttab manual_fe xt_fe, se ar2

Test joint significance of year dummies: (use test after the regression with year dummies)

* after reg fare_within share_within pass_within i.year
testparm i.year

Obtain within R^2 from xtreg output: Look at "R-sq: within" in xtreg output. To get more diagnostics:

xtreg log_fare bigcarrier_share log_passengers i.year, fe robust

If you need distance effect (between effect):

xtreg log_fare log_distance log_passengers bigcarrier_share, be

docs.title: 8 — A Short Troubleshooting Guide
docs.text: Problem Cause / Solution log() fails Check zeros/negative values with count if var <= 0. xtset complains Ensure route_id and year are properly formatted (numeric), sorted, and unique per panel/time. xtreg drops a variable Often because the variable is time-invariant (distance) or perfectly collinear with dummies. Manual within not matching xtreg Check you demeaned exactly the same variables and that no observations were lost (e.g., due to missing values).

docs.title: 9 — Save & Close
docs.text:
At the end of your session save the cleaned / transformed dataset and close the log:

save "AIRFARE_session4_working.dta", replace
log close

docs.title: Summary — What You Should Be Able to Explain After This Session
docs.text:
• How to construct logged variables and why.
  • The logic of the within (demeaning) transformation and how to compute it manually.
  • That the manual within OLS and xtreg, fe produce the same estimates for time-varying regressors.
  • Why time-invariant regressors (distance) disappear in the within estimator and how to obtain between estimates if needed.
  • The role of year dummies (two-way FE) and how to interpret the within R^2 change.
  • How to interpret coefficients on market share and log passengers as within effects (elasticities or approximate percent changes depending on units).

docs.title: STATA Tutorial: Event Studies – Google Stock (Session 5)
docs.text: 📌 Note:  All the full STATA codes used in this tutorial, together with training exercises and questions, are available for download on your Moodle page. Be sure to retrieve them so you can follow along and practice.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Hey everyone! 👋 In this session, we’re going to play the role of market detectives. We’re going to see how the stock market reacted to Google’s big announcement on August 10, 2015—when Google reorganized under Alphabet.

Event studies are a neat tool in finance and econometrics. The idea is simple: compare what actually happened (the stock’s return) with what we expected to happen if nothing special occurred. The difference? That’s called the abnormal return (AR), and it tells us how the market responded to the event.

We’ll go through three ways to measure abnormal returns, visualize them, and focus on the day of the announcement. Let's dive in!

💡 Tip: Think of abnormal returns as the “surprise” in the stock price caused by the event.

docs.title: 1. Getting Started
docs.text:
First, let’s clean our workspace and set the folder where our files live:

clear all
cd "C:\Users\ebada\Desktop\STATA S5"  // replace with your path

It’s always a good idea to log your session so you can revisit your work later:

log using "log_stata_session5.log", replace

docs.title: 2. Loading the Dataset
docs.text:
We’re using google_stock.dta, which has daily returns for Google and the S\&P 500 from May to August 2015.

causaldata google_stock.dta, use clear
describe

Take a look at the dataset. Notice the daily returns for Google (google_return) and the market (sp500_return). These are the building blocks for our abnormal return calculations.

docs.title: 3. Time Series Setup
docs.text:
Because this is daily data, we need to tell Stata it’s a time series:

tsset date

Now Stata knows we’re dealing with time-ordered data. This lets us plot returns over time easily.

docs.title: 4. Defining Estimation and Event Periods
docs.text:
Before calculating abnormal returns, we need two periods:

  1. Estimation period: This is our “normal” period before the event. We use it to figure out what Google’s returns normally look like.
  2. Observation period: This is around the event, where we measure abnormal returns.
gen est_period = date < td(01aug2015)
gen obs_period = inrange(date, td(01aug2015), td(31aug2015))

Think of it as: we’re learning Google’s “usual behavior” first, then checking how it reacts to the surprise.

docs.title: 5. Abnormal Returns – Mean Method
docs.text:
The simplest way to get abnormal returns is to compare daily returns to the pre-event average:

summarize google_return if est_period
gen mean_google = r(mean)

gen AR_mean = google_return - mean_google
label var AR_mean "Abnormal Return (Mean method)"

So here, we’re just saying: “What’s different today from the usual Google return?”

docs.title: 6. Abnormal Returns – Market Method
docs.text:
Next, we account for general market movements. If the whole market is up or down, we don’t want to confuse that with Google’s reaction.

gen AR_market = google_return - sp500_return
label var AR_market "Abnormal Return (Market method)"

Now the abnormal return is the difference between Google’s return and the S\&P 500 return.

docs.title: 7. Abnormal Returns – Risk-Adjusted Method
docs.text:
The risk-adjusted method is a bit fancier. We model Google’s return based on market movements (regression) and then calculate the surprise:

regress google_return sp500_return if est_period
predict expected_ret, xb

gen AR_risk = google_return - expected_ret
label var AR_risk "Abnormal Return (Risk-adjusted method)"

Here, we’re asking: “Given the market’s move today, how much did Google deviate from expectation?”

docs.title: 8. Visualizing Abnormal Returns
docs.text:
Graphs are your friends—they make patterns obvious. Let’s start with risk-adjusted abnormal returns for August 2015:

tsline AR_risk if obs_period, tline(10aug2015) ///
    title("Abnormal Return – Google (August 2015)") ///
    ytitle("Abnormal Return") ///
    yscale(range(-.06 .06)) ylabel(-.06(.02).06, angle(0) format(%4.2f)) ///
    xtitle("Date")

graph export "AR_risk_Google_August2015.png", replace

Now let’s compare all three methods in one plot:

tsline AR_mean AR_market AR_risk if obs_period, tline(10aug2015) ///
    title("Abnormal Returns (Different Methods)") ///
    legend(order(1 "Mean" 2 "Market" 3 "Risk-adjusted")) ///
    ytitle("Abnormal Return") ///
    yscale(range(-.06 .06)) ylabel(-.06(.02).06, angle(0) format(%4.2f)) ///
    xtitle("Date")

graph export "AR_comparison_Google_August2015.png", replace

See how the abnormal returns spike on August 10? That’s the market reacting to the announcement.

docs.title: 9. Inspecting the Event Day
docs.text:
Curious about the exact numbers on the announcement day?

list date google_return AR_mean AR_market AR_risk if date==td(10aug2015), noobs

Now you can see the actual return and how “abnormal” it was according to each method.

docs.title: 10. Interpreting Abnormal Returns
docs.text:
Alright, now that we have our abnormal returns and graphs, let’s talk about what they actually mean. Remember: abnormal returns are the difference between what happened and what we expected.

Positive AR: The stock did better than expected. For Google on August 10, a positive spike would mean the market reacted favorably to the announcement.

Negative AR: The stock did worse than expected. A drop tells us investors were surprised negatively or worried about the news.

Compare the three methods:

Mean method: Simple, just compares against the average historical return. Quick and intuitive, but doesn’t account for market-wide movements.

Market method: Adjusts for the overall market movement. This helps isolate Google-specific effects from general market swings.

Risk-adjusted method: The most sophisticated of the three. It accounts for Google’s typical sensitivity to the market. If Google usually moves with the market, this method tells us whether today’s move was unusual even given the market’s movement.

💡 Tip: Look at the spike on August 10 in your graphs. A clear positive or negative peak indicates that the announcement had a meaningful impact. The bigger the spike, the stronger the market reaction.

Also, check the magnitude of the abnormal returns:

Small AR (~0.5%) may indicate a mild reaction.

Large AR (>2–3%) usually signals a major market reaction.

Finally, compare across methods. If all three methods show a similar spike, that’s strong evidence the event mattered. If they differ, consider market conditions or estimation assumptions—sometimes, choosing the right benchmark makes a difference.

docs.title: 11. Closing Your Session
docs.text:
Don’t forget to save your work:

log close
